_about: Monthly follow-up calls (about 10 to 15 minutes each, one topic per call, for about 6 months), the way Pillway's pharmacists run them. Sarah covers ONE topic per follow-up, in this order, skipping topics marked skip_if. Facts come from Diabetes Canada (see each source). Edit freely: questions are guides, not a script.

topics.goal: Help them add fibre gradually: whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruit with skins.

questions.en: What does a usual breakfast and lunch look like for you?
Which of these do you eat most weeks: beans or lentils, oats or barley, whole grain bread, nuts and seeds?
What is one small fibre swap you'd like to try this month?

facts: Include both soluble fibre (oats, barley, legumes, apples, carrots) and insoluble fibre (whole grains, nuts and seeds, fruit and vegetable skins, leafy greens).
Add fibre in small amounts over time and drink more water, to avoid an upset stomach.
Fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables; choose whole grains more often; check labels for fibre.

topics.goal: Build a daily foot check habit and know when to call for help.

questions.en: How often do you look at your feet, including between the toes and the soles?
Have you noticed any cuts, blisters, colour changes, numbness or tingling lately?
What kind of shoes and socks do you usually wear around the house and outside?

facts: Check feet every day (a mirror helps for the soles); wash and dry well, especially between the toes.
Wear well-fitting shoes and clean socks; don't walk barefoot.
Any sore that isn't healing, new colour change or numbness should be seen by a health-care provider.

topics.goal: Work toward 150 minutes a week of activity they enjoy, plus some strength work.

questions.en: How active were you this past week, and what did you do?
What kind of movement do you actually enjoy, or used to?
What's a realistic goal for the next month?

facts: Aim for at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity (for example 30 minutes, 5 days a week); 10-minute bouts count.
Try not to go more than 2 days in a row without activity; add strength exercises 2 to 3 times a week.
Start low and go slow; anyone who has been inactive should check with their doctor before anything harder than a brisk walk.

topics.goal: Make sure they can recognise and are ready for a low.

questions.en: Have you had any lows since we last talked?
What does a low feel like for you, if you've had one?
Do you keep something fast-acting with you, like juice or glucose tablets?

facts: Below 4 mmol/L is considered low blood sugar.
If they feel low, check right away; if they can't check, treat it anyway.
Wait until blood sugar is above 5 mmol/L before driving. Repeated lows should be discussed with the pharmacist.

topics.goal: Get a yearly dilated eye exam booked and know the warning signs.

questions.en: Have you had an eye exam with drops in the past year?
Any blurry vision, flashes, or spots lately?
Would it help if your pharmacist reminded you to book one?

facts: People with diabetes should have an eye exam about once a year, or as their eye doctor advises.
Blurred vision, flashes of light, spots or sudden vision loss need an eye doctor right away.
Keeping A1C, blood pressure and cholesterol on target, not smoking and staying active protect the eyes.

topics.goal: Regular home readings and steady progress toward their target.

questions.en: Have you been able to check your blood pressure at home? What numbers are you seeing?
How much salty or processed food is in a usual week for you?
What would make checking it regularly easier?

facts: A common target for people with diabetes is below 130/80 mmHg; the pharmacist confirms each person's target.
Less salt and processed food, regular activity and limiting alcohol help lower blood pressure.

topics.goal: Check in on how they're coping and point to support.

questions.en: How have you been feeling lately, honestly?
Who do you lean on when things get hard?

facts: Feeling stressed or down about diabetes is common; it's okay to ask for help.
The pharmacist can connect them with support if stress is affecting daily life.

topics.goal: Meet them where they are (not ready / thinking / ready) and offer the pharmacist's help.

questions.en: Where are you with smoking these days?
Would you like your pharmacist to help you make a plan?

facts: Quitting smoking lowers the risk of heart, eye, kidney and foot problems.
Pharmacists can help with a quit plan and quit aids.
